text: A bank statement arriving at Oracle isn't a PDF — it's a structured data file in one of several standard formats. This lesson covers the three you'll see most often: BAI2, SWIFT MT940, and ISO 20022 CAMT.053.

BAI2 is the US standard: a plain text, line based format where each line starts with a type code. MT940 is a SWIFT message type used heavily outside the US, organized into tagged fields instead of fixed codes. CAMT.053 is part of the ISO 20022 family, XML based, and increasingly the long term replacement for MT940 in markets moving away from older SWIFT formats.

Here's a trimmed BAI2 snippet. Record 01 is the file header. Record 02 is the group header. Record 03 opens a specific account and carries its opening balance. Record 16 is one transaction detail line, each carrying a BAI2 transaction type code. Records 49, 98 and 99 are the account, group and file trailers.

And here's the MT940 equivalent, using tagged fields. Tag 20 is the transaction reference. Tag 25 identifies the account. Tag 60F is the opening balance. Tag 61 is one statement line per transaction. Tag 86 carries narrative detail for the line above it. Tag 62F is the closing balance.

A multinational company might see all three formats, depending on which bank and which country sends the statement — but Oracle loads every one of them into the same internal structure, so reconciliation downstream doesn't care which format arrived. Up next, lesson six: how these files actually get loaded and imported into Oracle.
